hook.text: A self-driving car needs to see the world—and cameras are the cheapest way to give it eyes.

buildup.text: Multiple cameras around the car stitch together a full 360-degree view of the surroundings.

discovery.text: Neural networks process the images in real time, identifying lanes, signs, cars, and pedestrians.

twist.text: Cameras fail in the same conditions human eyes do—glare, darkness, and heavy rain blind them.

climax.text: Tesla bet its entire self-driving strategy on cameras alone, while competitors added other sensors.

punchline.text: Cameras see everything cheaply but struggle when humans do too.

quiz.question: Which company bets entirely on cameras for self-driving, without lidar?

details.summary: Self-driving cars use arrays of cameras to capture visual data similar to human eyes, employing deep learning neural networks to identify lanes, signs, pedestrians, and obstacles in real time.
details.whyItMatters: Cameras are the cheapest and most information-rich sensors available. Tesla's decision to rely primarily on cameras sparked an industry debate about whether vision alone can achieve full autonomy.
takeaways: Camera arrays capture 360-degree views around the vehicle
Neural networks process millions of pixels per second to detect objects
Cameras struggle in darkness, glare, and heavy precipitation

faq.question: Can cameras replace lidar and radar entirely?
faq.answer: Tesla believes so, using a vision-only approach. Most other companies disagree, arguing that cameras cannot reliably measure distance or function well in all lighting and weather conditions without supplemental sensors.

faq.question: How do cameras identify objects they have never seen before?
faq.answer: Neural networks generalize from millions of training examples. If a camera sees an unusual obstacle, the model compares it to learned patterns. Novel objects remain a challenge, which is why edge cases are so difficult.
